definition: Cyclical means occurring in repeating cycles or regularly recurring patterns.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cyclical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cyclical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The bay's crab harvest is cyclical, fat seasons and lean ones taking turns in a rhythm the old captains can feel coming.
A recurring problem simply keeps showing up; cyclical promises a shaped loop — away, back, and away again on a rhythm.
Metronomic goes past cyclical — the return is not just regular but machine-exact, tick after identical tick.

Rhythmic describes a beat you can hear or feel — a drum, an oar stroke, a heartbeat — pulse following pulse in quick succession. Cyclical claims something slower and larger: a loop that swings away and comes back, sometimes taking years to come around once.

Seasonal ties a pattern to the calendar's seasons — strawberries in June, flu each winter — so the return always rides a particular time of year. Cyclical is broader: its loop can run on any period at all, long or short, with no season attached.

Cyclical means occurring in repeating cycles or regularly recurring patterns.
In the far north, lemming populations boom and bust on a beat of roughly four years, and the snowy owls that eat them boom and bust a step behind.
Field notebooks going back a century of winters trace the same rising and falling line again and again: the system is cyclical, and the birds are bound to it as tightly as the seasons.
Cyclical is the exact word because it names what occurs in repeating cycles or regularly recurring patterns — movement that swings away and comes back on a rhythm.
Recurring says only that a thing happens again; cyclical adds the shape of the loop, the swing away and back that a graph shows tracing itself over and over.
Reach for cyclical when a pattern swings away and reliably comes back around.

Its neighbors in this unit divide the territory: sequential orders steps in a line that runs once; sporadic scatters events with no rhythm at all; and when the sameness has merely gone dull, the complaint you want is monotonous.

When Mara opened her vintage shop, she assumed the racks of wide-legged jeans from the nineties would sit unsold forever.
Her grandmother, who had run the shop before her, only laughed and told her to wait.
Style, the old woman said, is cyclical: what walks out of fashion keeps walking, comes all the way around, and walks back in — the loop just takes about twenty years to close.
Sure enough, by the shop's third year, teenagers were paying triple for the same jeans their parents had once donated in embarrassment.
Mara stopped throwing anything away.
Now she tags each unfashionable crate with the decade she expects it to come back, like a gardener labeling bulbs.
